article_title: ClickHouse Says It Scaled Near-Linearly Across Vera's 176 Physical Cores in In-Memory Benchmarks and Topped the ClickBench Hardware Leaderboard

content_preview.title: ClickHouse Says It Scaled Near-Linearly Across Vera's 176 Physical Cores in In-Memory Benchmarks and Topped the ClickBench Hardware Leaderboard
content_preview.summary: In a blog post, ClickHouse reports that three CPU-bound micro-benchmarks scaled close to linearly up to 176 threads on an early-access NVIDIA Vera server, with efficiency falling beyond that.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

ClickHouse published an engineering post on October 21, 2026, describing how its database performed on an early-access server built on NVIDIA's upcoming Vera CPU. In the [ClickHouse blog](https://clickhouse.com/blog/clickhouse-performance-on-nvidia-vera), author Robert Schulze writes that the company ran ClickBench, its analytics benchmark, on the machine and that "NVIDIA Vera immediately made it to the top of the ClickBench hardware leaderboard by a wide margin." The post then goes...

editor_notes.content_quality: Clear News piece (872 words, within 400-1200). Structure: overview, setup, per-benchmark results, SIMD/agentic context, explicit 'What We Don't Know' section. Every figure is attributed to ClickHouse's post and flagged as not independently reproduced; early-access hardware is stated.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read all three snapshots (source-0/1/2.html.gz), manifest suspicious_patterns null for all, status 200. source-0 (clickhouse.com blog, Robert Schulze, Oct 21 2026): confirmed verbatim 'NVIDIA Vera immediately made it to the top of the ClickBench hardware leaderboard by a wide margin' (an unquantified first-party claim; no leaderboard figures in the post), 'the standard ClickHouse binary from our website', 88 Olympus cores / Arm-v9.2 / 176 cores / 352 hardware threads in a two-socket system / 1.0-1.2 TB/s, 62.5 billion strings 1 TB uncompressed Memory engine; all table figures checked individually against raw text: LIKE 50.44s->1.23s@64 (41.01x), 1.11s@256, 813 GB/s; regex 1209.7->7.4s@176 (163.47x, 92.88%), 5.3s@352 (228.25x, 64.84%); aggregation 884.1->5.4s@176 (163.72x, 93.02%), 4.9s at 256 and 352 (180.43x); join 1132.6->7.3s@176 (155.15x, 88.15%), 6.1s at 256 and 352; quotes 'scale almost perfectly with the number of CPU cores' and 'In other words, ClickHouse scales perfectly' verbatim; efficiency decline past 176 cores due to SMT, 10-30% for compute-bound; SIMD 0.42s vs 1.48s ('3.5x slower'), NEON, SVE2 PR #122860; agentic-query description; Milovidov quote verbatim ('NVIDIA Vera is an incredibly fast and powerful server platform - the fastest we have seen so far'). Live re-fetch via curl returned identical content (same byte size 437952; key strings re-grepped). The post says NVIDIA 'provided us with an early-access server' (vendor-supplied hardware, first-party benchmark). Title scope: 'near-linearly' holds for the three CPU-bound tests up to 176 threads (equal to physical cores in the machine); the first LIKE test was memory-bound and did not scale, which the body and summary state. 'Topped the leaderboard' is an attributed claim under the 'ClickHouse Says...' title scope. I also checked the live ClickBench hardware leaderboard data (benchmark.clickhouse.com/hardware): an entry 'NVIDIA Vera (Olympus)' exists, and my rough geometric-mean ratio of best-of-3 times ranked it first (about 1.10 vs 1.15 for the next, AWS r9gd.48xlarge Graviton5); this is my own approximation, not the official metric, and does not confirm or quantify a 'wide margin'. source-1 (nvidia.com Vera page): '88 custom NVIDIA Olympus cores' and 'up to 1.2 terabytes per second (TB/s) of LPDDR5X memory bandwidth' confirmed in raw text (page also says SMT creates 176 threads per CPU, consistent with 2x88 cores/352 threads in a dual-socket system). source-2 (duckdb.org, Oct 16): confirmed 'the Vera platform has a 46% performance advantage on TPC-H SF1,000 over the x86 baseline (Intel Xeon 6)' (article's quote is a verbatim fragment), single socket via numactl with threads=88, preview build; page states the work was 'in collaboration with the NVIDIA team'. Internal link /article/2026-10/19-duckdb-benchmarks-its-v20-preview-on-nvidia-vera-... resolves to an existing article and is described accurately; the article does not compare ClickHouse and DuckDB results as like-for-like and in fact notes the different thread/socket scope. Hostnames clickhouse.com, nvidia.com (www.nvidia.com covered by the apex entry) and duckdb.org are on config/source_allowlist.txt; no allowlist edit needed. Body URLs match article.sources exactly (3/3, no orphans). validate:content run (see below).
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No fabricated or misattributed specifics found. Arithmetic and every quoted number match the raw post text. Minor imprecision only: 'Vera's 176 physical cores' in the title refers to the two-socket server, not a single Vera CPU (88 cores); the body states the two-socket configuration.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral; claims consistently attributed ('the post says', 'ClickHouse reports'); no editorializing.
editor_notes.originality: New story. Related prior coverage is the DuckDB-on-Vera article (2026-10/19), linked in the body and listed as a related article; different vendor, different benchmark, different angle.
concerns: First-party source: the central claims (scaling and the ClickBench leaderboard position) come from ClickHouse's own engineering blog and are unreplicated; the article states this.

Vendor collaboration: NVIDIA supplied the early-access server and ClickHouse's post promotes the platform; the NVIDIA page is also a vendor source. Only the NVIDIA-supplied hardware is stated in the post, not any financial arrangement. The article says 'early-access' but does not say NVIDIA provided the machine; readers see the first-party framing via attribution but not that explicit fact.
Title compresses scope: 'Near-Linearly' applies to three CPU-bound tests, not the memory-bound LIKE test; body and summary carry the qualification.
'Wide margin' on ClickBench is unquantified in the post; my own rough check shows Vera first on the leaderboard but could not confirm the size of the margin.
recommendations: For similar pieces, state in the body who supplied the hardware when the source says so.
Prefer an independent source (leaderboard data or third-party reproduction) alongside first-party benchmark claims.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Accurate, carefully hedged coverage of a first-party benchmark post; all numbers and quotes verified against raw source text, headline claims properly attributed through 'ClickHouse Says'. Verdict APPROVE with the first-party and vendor-collaboration concerns documented. Featured candidacy: 1 - accurate vendor benchmark coverage of interest to database and hardware engineers, but first-party and niche
